l: (Joan looks up over her half-moon glasses, a telephone tucked under her chin.) Well, look who's back. Chuck's had me watching the door since seven. (She puts the telephone down.) How was the leave? No, don't tell me. You'll only make me jealous.

You too. Nothing changes: Chuck's upstairs, the coffee's still terrible, and Doris wants you in the Cover Story Department first, through the door on the left. Wherever he's sending you, you're not going as yourself.
(Joan doesn't stop typing.) You know the way: Cover Story's through the door on the left, Chuck's up the stairs, and the coffee's in the cafeteria. I still wouldn't.
(Peggy grins.) Back for more? I'm flying you, wherever it is. We're not going anywhere until Chuck's had his talk with you, upstairs. Then she's all yours.
My name is Chuck. I work at Chuck's Office. I like CIA.
(Doris looks you up and down.) You again. Sit down, let's have a look at you. Hair, clothes, the lot: wherever Chuck's sending you this time, you're not going in a government suit.

There you are. Sit down. Good to have you back. Like the new look. You're going to Sarivalto, an island in the Baltic. Snow, fish, cola and not much else. Its king has just died, and right now nobody knows who's going to run the place.

Everyone. The Communists want the island in the Soviet Union, and Moscow would love a harbour that far north. The royals want the crown kept on Prince Leopold's head. Kelp Cola wants whoever's best for business. The Democrats want a vote. And there's an oil company and a syndicate sniffing around too.

An island that doesn't end up flying a red flag. Your codename is NIGHTJAR. Your cover's a British reporter, from a London paper, there to cover the king's death, so ask all the questions you like. When you're settled in, go and introduce yourself to the island's newspaper, the Eastbrook Gazette: a reporter would. Our man there is Hekki, the radio tech: he's fixed you up a room under his shack, at the radio tower, with a radio set and a screen to reach me on.
You fly out for the first of September, and the island's yours for thirty days. Talk to everyone, help the people who'll help us, and call me every morning. Good luck, NIGHTJAR.
Me again: I'm your ride. It's a long way to the Baltic, and we don't land anywhere anyone can see: a fishing boat meets us off the island at dawn and takes you the rest of the way in. Ready?
(Sam is mending a net on an upturned crate. He nods.) Reporter.
My father's. He knotted it in 1931. I'm mending it. A knot at a time.
(Kaisa slides the headphones off one ear.) Radio Sarivalto, live and slightly out of tune. I'm Kaisa. You're the reporter, the whole island's heard. Don't touch the red button.
Everyone. Communists, monks, oil men. It's the only thing we agree on.
(Hekki looks both ways along the path, twice.) You're NIGHTJAR. You must be. You look exactly like a British reporter, which is the idea, I suppose. I'm Hekki. Radio. And, well. The other thing.
(He drops to a whisper.) Sorry. Sorry. I've been practising. Your room's under my shack: the bookcase, third shelf. Lean on it. It swings.

Radio sets, tape recorders, a bed, a stove, and more tinned soup than one person needs. And the radio set, for calling Chuck: tune it in and call him the minute you're down there. He'll want to hear you've landed. (He swallows.) Welcome to Sarivalto, NIGHTJAR.
"Sorry, I can't think straight. You don't have any food on you, do you?" you ask. Then you've come to the right person. Have a look at what I've got.
(Chuck's voice, thin through the static.) NIGHTJAR, Langley. Good to hear you. Did you make it in one piece?
In one piece. Hekki says hello.

Good. First job: the Communist Party. They want this island in the Soviet Union, and that's exactly what we're here to stop. Their leader is a woman called Anna, at their HQ in Saltwick. Go and talk to her. Friendly. Find out where they stand, and don't tip your hand. Over.
Comrade! Not many come in from the cold to visit us. What brings you to the Party's door?
A journalist! Then write this down: Sarivalto's future lies with the Soviet Union. Moscow will give this island what its kings never did.
NIGHTJAR. You saw Anna? What's the Party really after?
She wants the island in the Soviet Union, and she means it.
That's what I was afraid of. A true believer's harder to deal with than a man with a price. Good work. Get some sleep: tomorrow, Kingsgrad.
(Tiina doesn't look up.) Sirpa's told you everything already, I expect. She'll have told you my name's Tiina. That's all you need to know today.
Is it? You don't know me yet. Wait a week. (The corner of her mouth moves.)
Go on. Sirpa's got more to say than I have.
(Sirpa looks you up and down.) Well! You came in on Tom's boat this morning. Don't look like that: I see everything that comes up this street. Sirpa. And you're the reporter.
Anna's had the Party lights on since five, Lucia came home at three in the morning with sand on her shoes, and Hannu's selling last week's paper again.
(Ray looks you up and down, the way she looks at everyone, and then puts a glass on the bar.) You're the first stranger through that door since the snow came. What'll it be?
Whisky, then. It's the only thing in Saltwick that's been warm since August.
(Hannu snaps his paper shut and beams.) A reporter! Splendid. Colleague, in a manner of speaking. I sell the news. You write it. Between us we're an industry.
'King Dead, Island Mourns.' It was true yesterday and it'll be true tomorrow. A solid story. Keeps its shape.
(Anna is pinning a map of the island to the wall, with Saltwick shaded red.) Only Saltwick's dug out so far, comrade, so only Saltwick matters today. The rest of the island is still under the snow.
Because it's ours: fishermen, gutters, dockers. By the end of the month I'd like a great many more red pins.

Morning, NIGHTJAR. Good work on Anna. The snow's cleared on the road to Kingsgrad, so today it's the palace. The old king's dead, and whoever ends up wearing the crown, or tearing it down, matters to us. Meet the family: Prince Leopold, his brother Augustus and his sister Daphne. And talk to the staff, every one of them. Butlers and maids hear everything.
Good. Be polite, be curious, and remember who said what.

(Hekki watches you squint down the road.) NIGHTJAR, can I say something? You've walked past my tower three times this morning. A spy should know where they are. Hannu sells maps at his newsstand in Saltwick. Three dollars. Will you get one?
Good. Bring it here and I'll mark a few things on it. Small marks. Nothing anyone would notice.
(Hannu shuffles his papers.) Kingsgrad's open. That means a thick Gazette, and a thicker rumour. A man from the palace was seen buying a very large bouquet.
A man told me who told a man. It's all very above board.
(Hekki unfolds it across his knees and takes out a pencil.) Oh, it's the good one. With the contour lines. May I?
(He draws a very small circle.) The Radio Tower. That's us. And a dot by the harbour, where the boats come in at night. If anyone asks, they're places I like the view.

The snow's still blocking the roads north and east. They'll open a bit at a time. Look at the map from your bag whenever you're lost, and you won't walk past my tower again. (He folds it back up, wrongly.)
Kingsgrad's open. (He doesn't look up.) Don't need anything in Kingsgrad.
Once. 1952. Took herring to the kitchens. Cook gave me a bun. Good bun.
(Pat holds up a green glass bottle, corked and waxed.) Look what the sea sent me. There's a letter in it. In Russian, I think: all backwards Rs.
Not yet. You open a thing like that, it stops being a mystery and starts being someone's business. I'm enjoying the mystery.
If you can read Russian, keep it to yourself for now. I like not knowing.
Morning! Oskar, footman. I open the doors, carry the bags and stand very still in the cold. Mostly the cold.
Visitors I've never seen before, coming up the drive late at night. Men in good coats. Mr Edmund says I didn't see them, so I didn't.
Mind the hedges. Viktor. I keep the grounds, such as they are under all this snow.
Do you see much out here?
Everything comes and goes by the front gate, and the front gate goes past my shed. I don't say. Nobody asks a gardener.
A new face! Walk with me, the gardens are the only place in the palace where the walls don't have ears. Well, Viktor has ears, but he only uses them for birdsong.
Who would listen at the walls?
Everyone, darling. The Party, the Americans, the cola people, my own brothers. Half the island wants something from this family, and the other half wants it gone. I find it terribly exciting.
(Oskar stamps his feet on the step.) Sorry. Can't feel my toes. They're in there somewhere, I counted them this morning.
Saving for them. Harbour Outfitters in Saltwick have fur-lined ones, real sheepskin. I'm a third of the way there. The left one, roughly.
You'll want to stand back, this is all starch. Elsa. Every sheet and shirt in the palace comes through this room.
Hard on the hands, easy on the head. And nobody notices a laundress.
Out of my way unless you're carrying onions. Marta. I cook for the family, the staff and every hungry fool who wanders into my kitchen.
What does the prince like to eat?
Herring, like his father. Daphne eats nothing and says it's delicious. Augustus fasts on saints' days, and he's found a lot of saints lately.
Mind the tablecloth, it's just been pressed. Lotta. I set the dining room and clear it again.
They sit together. They don't talk together. It's a long table.
Shh. This is a library. Oh, you're new. Augustus. The other brother. The one who reads.
The lives of the saints. Father Thyme at the monastery lends them to me. They all suffered beautifully. I've not got the knack of it yet.
Good morning. Edmund, butler to the household these thirty-one years. If you've business with the family, you have it through me.
You must know the palace better than anyone.
I know every room, every key and every secret in it, sir. Which is precisely why I keep them.
You'll forgive me if I don't stand. My father's chair is larger than it looks. Are you here to offer condolences, or advice? I've had a great deal of both.

If the island lets me. There are people in Saltwick who'd rather bury the crown with him, and people in Eastbrook who'd sell it. I mean to be crowned. Whether I'm king of anything afterwards is another question.
Oh! I wasn't listening, I was dusting. Ingrid. I keep the royal apartments.
Is it a good place to work?
It's warm and the food's good. You keep your head down and your apron clean.
(Lisa beams from behind the till.) Oh! You're new. You're the reporter, aren't you? From London? Actual London?
I knew it! The coat. Nobody here has a coat like that. Is it true there are shops on every street? Shops on top of shops?
NIGHTJAR. You've been through the whole palace? Tell me what you've got.
Leopold means to be crowned, whatever it takes.
Then he's either our best friend on this island or our biggest headache. We'll find out which. Good work: that's the household on file.
